newsitem.title: CONGO: Neighbour Congo feels effect of Zaire war.
newsitem.headline: Neighbour Congo feels effect of Zaire war.

text.p: Zaire's civil war has sent prices soaring in the markets of Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo, and sent a shiver of apprehension through its population of 950,000 people.

A steady flow of Zaireans across the River Zaire from their capital Kinshasa, in search of supplies or refuge, has proved a boon for Brazzaville's hoteliers and traders -- and even its customs officers.
But officials say the government, aware that the same four km (2.5 mile) of water could bring far less welcome side-effects, has set up a crisis committee.
Kinshasa's citizens, prey to shortages in the face of a sustained advance by rebels seeking to topple veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, cross the river by boat to shop for food.

They return with milk, butter, potatoes, fresh and salted fish, meat, chicken and rice. Residents say a 15,000 CFA franc sack of rice now costs 20,000 CFA in Brazzaville -- and the equivalent of 25,000 CFA in Kinshasa.
Other prices have also risen, under pressure of demand from across the river.

On Brazzaville Beach, the river port, dozens of top of the range cars from Zaire are sold on the black market. Diplomatic vehicles are parked there in anticipation that Kinshasa will one day return to normal.
Some Zairean families have moved out, bringing their furniture with them, in search of security in Brazzaville.

Government officials decline to release details of the discussions of the crisis committee, which was set up to plan for any eventuality. Since the start of the week, it has held frequent meetings, officials say.
The Congolese navy has been on alert for a couple of months. Soldiers monitor the national borders along the city's river front.
On the river itself, troops from Belgium, France, the United States or Britain mount patrols in light craft -- occasionally practising rescue exercises.
In the event of a collapse of law and order in Kinshasa, they will have the job of rescuing their nationals.
Travellers say that across the river on the Zairean side members of Mobutu's presidential guard, the one force likely to stand between Mobutu and the rebels, keep a close watch on their activities.
